mcp.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server
mcp.blurb: Connect autonomous AI agents (Antigravity, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code with Roo Code/Cline, or local models via Ollama/LM Studio) directly to PZ Mod Studio. The MCP server gives them the console log, crash reports, the files two mods both replace, a Lua syntax check and control of the running game.
mcp.generatorBlurb: Select your AI client or environment and copy the JSON snippet into your configuration file:
mcp.important: Important: Do NOT run pz-mcp-server.exe directly by double-clicking
mcp.importantBlurb: If you double-click pz-mcp-server.exe, a black command prompt will open and stay blank. This is completely normal. The MCP server communicates silently over stdio (JSON-RPC) with AI agents. You do not need to keep it open; your AI assistant (Claude, Cursor, Antigravity) will launch and close it automatically in the background whenever you send prompts in chat.

claude.title: How to set it up in Claude Desktop:
claude.s1: Open Claude Desktop and go to File > Settings (or press Ctrl + ,).
claude.s2: Select the Developer tab and click Edit Config to open claude_desktop_config.json.
claude.s3: Paste the JSON configuration above inside the file and save it.
claude.s4: Restart Claude Desktop. In new chats you will see a 🔨 Hammer icon with the PZ Mod Studio tools.
claude.tip: 💬 Example prompt: "Read console.txt to diagnose why Project Zomboid crashed" or "Sort my mod load order".

cursor.title: How to set it up in Cursor / Windsurf:
cursor.s4: The status dot turns green (Enabled) and the agent can use the Studio's tools.
cursor.tip: 💬 Example prompt: "@pz-mod-studio find the files my active mods both replace and merge the scripts".

vscode.title: How to set it up in VS Code (Roo Code / Cline, with local or cloud models):
vscode.s1: Install the Roo Code or Cline extension from the VS Code Marketplace.
vscode.s2: Click the extension's icon in the sidebar, open the MCP Servers tab at the top and choose Configure MCP.
vscode.s4: Cloud models work, and so do local ones with Ollama / LM Studio (e.g. Qwen 2.5 Coder).
vscode.tip: 🔒 Offline: with a local model, the Studio's tools (file conflicts, Lua checks, logs) work without an internet connection.

antigravity.title: How to set it up in Antigravity / Gemini CLI:
antigravity.s1: Open your Antigravity or Gemini CLI settings file (.gemini/settings.json or the user settings).
antigravity.s2: Paste the snippet under the "mcpServers" section.
antigravity.s3: Antigravity finds and connects every tool and resource on its own.
antigravity.tip: 💬 Example prompt: "Read console.txt and tell me which mod is failing and how to fix it".

openai.title: How to set it up in OpenAI / Codex / other MCP bridges:
openai.s1: Point your MCP client or local stdio bridge at the executable as its command.
openai.s2: The server describes its tools following the JSON-RPC 2.0 MCP standard (2024-11-05).
openai.s3: Make sure the process is started with standard input and output pipes (stdio).

keptVersions.title: Keep earlier versions of mods
keptVersions.blurb: Steam keeps no old versions of a Workshop mod: an update replaces the files. The Studio keeps a copy of the installed version of every Workshop mod a profile uses, before Steam replaces it, so a broken update can be undone from the Mod List (right click, Versions). Each file is kept once, so a version after an update costs only what changed. Past the limit, the oldest versions go first; versions you keep by hand stay. Whatever the limit, the drive is always left with 15% of its size free. Never while the game runs.

bisect.startConfirm:
Start halving your mod list?

{{count}} mods are switched on. The hunt switches half of them off, you play, and it halves again until one mod is left — about 8 launches for a list this size.

Your list is kept and put back when the hunt ends, whichever way it ends.
bisect.title: Find the mod that does it
bisect.intro: For what the log cannot tell you: a freeze, a recipe that never shows, a save that will not open. Part of your mods is tried, you play, and the part that still fails is cut down. About 8 launches find one mod in a hundred, and also a pair of mods that fail only together. Mods this PC already suspects are tried first.
bisect.confirming: One mod is left: {{mod}}, and it is the only suspect switched on. Play, then say whether it still happens.
bisect.trial: {{trial}} of {{candidates}} suspects are switched on, plus the {{alwaysOn}} mods another mod requires. Play the way you did when it happened, then answer.
bisect.owns: The hunt owns the mod list until it ends: switching mods on or off in the Mod List while it runs makes the next answer mean nothing.
bisect.saveOwnList: A saved game loads with its own mod list, not the trial's: start a new game for each trial. If you load an old one, the Studio Link says which mods it brings back that the trial switched off; taking them out changes that save (a backup is kept).
bisect.giveUp: Stop and put my list back
bisect.culprit: It is {{mod}}. It was the only suspect switched on and it still happened, in {{launches}} launches. Your list is back on.
bisect.patchFileTitle: Open {{file}} in the Merger and patch it
bisect.logNeverNames: The log never names it, which is what the hunt is for. There is no line to point at, so what to patch is yours to find: its files can still be opened.
bisect.showLines: Show its lines in the console
bisect.patchAnyTitle: Open its files in the Merger. The mod stays on; the package loads last, so the game reads your copy of the file you patch.
bisect.flaky: Does not happen every time: a "no longer happens" is tried twice before it is believed
bisect.targetPlaceholder: Optional: some text of the error as the log writes it
bisect.targetHelp: With a text, after each test game the app reads the log and suggests the answer.
bisect.pairSearch: {{mod}} on its own does not do it: it stays on in every trial while the mod that does it together with it is sought.
bisect.leads: Starts with what this PC already suspects: {{mods}}.
bisect.goneOnce: As it does not happen every time, this same trial runs once more before "no longer happens" is believed.
bisect.suggestStill: The test game's log shows the error: it looks like it still happens.
bisect.suggestGone: The test game's log loaded the save and does not show the error: it looks like it no longer happens.
bisect.culpritPair: It is {{mod}} and {{other}} together: neither does it on its own, both do. {{launches}} launches. Your list is back.
bisect.confirmNone: Now a trial with none of the suspects (only what must stay on). If it still happens, it is none of these mods; if it no longer does, it is {{mod}}.

require.nowhere: No module called {{wanted}} exists in the game or in any mod you have switched on. The mod is asking for something that is not there: either it needs another mod you do not have, or it is a bug for its author.
require.samePath: {{owner}} has {{path}} at exactly that path, in {{phase}}/. The file is there, so what failed is where it was asked from: the game loads shared first, then client, then server. shared cannot see client or server, and client cannot see server (on a dedicated server client/ is not loaded at all). Changing the path does not fix it.
require.gameMovedNoise: The game has this module at {{path}} (in {{phase}}/), not at {{wanted}}. No error from this file follows this line in the log.
require.gameMovedFailed: The game has this module at {{path}} (in {{phase}}/), not at {{wanted}}. Further down the log {{file}} fails, so here it matters: fixing the path is what mends it.
require.moved: A module of that name is in {{owner}}, at {{path}} (in {{phase}}/), not at {{wanted}}. If it is the one this mod wants, changing that line to ask for that path fixes it; if {{owner}} has nothing to do with this mod, it may be a different module with the same name.
require.optional: {{mod}} asks for a module ({{wanted}}) that is not in the game or in any mod you have installed. The game carried on, and no error from {{file}} follows in the log: it looks like an optional link to another mod. Nothing to do.
require.optionalOff: {{mod}} asks for a module of {{owner}} ({{wanted}}), which you have installed and switched off. The game carried on, and no error from {{file}} follows in the log: it looks like an optional link between the two. Nothing to do.
require.nowhereOff: No module called {{wanted}} is in the game or in the mods you have switched on. {{owner}}, which you have installed and switched off, has it at that path.
require.movedUnrelated: A module of that name is in {{owner}}, at {{path}} (in {{phase}}/), not at {{wanted}}. Neither mod asks for the other, so it may be a different module with the same name: nothing is fixed from here.

health.duplicate_entry: {{mod}} is in the active list more than once
health.missing_mod_similar: {{mod}} is not installed. Mod ids are case-sensitive: did you mean {{similar}}?
health.missing_mod_gone: {{mod}} is enabled but not installed (unsubscribed or deleted)
health.not_for_build_some: {{mod}} has no files for game build {{build}} (it has: {{folders}}). The game will not load it.
health.not_for_build_none: {{mod}} has no files for game build {{build}} (it has: nothing usable{{folders}}). The game will not load it.
health.outside_version_range: {{mod}} supports game versions {{min}} to {{max}}; you have {{build}}. The game will not load it.
health.missing_dependency_similar: {{mod}} requires {{dep}}, which is not installed (an installed mod is called {{similar}}: ids are case-sensitive)
health.dependency_not_enabled: {{mod}} requires {{dep}}, which is installed but off in this list. The game loads it anyway, as a requirement, so nothing breaks; switch it on so the list shows what runs.
health.dependency_unavailable_not_installed: {{mod}} requires {{dep}}, which is unavailable: {{culprit}} is not installed
health.dependency_unavailable_cannot_load: {{mod}} requires {{dep}}, which is unavailable: {{culprit}} cannot load on this build
health.load_after_order: {{mod}} asks to load after {{other}}, but {{other}} loads later
health.load_before_order: {{mod}} asks to load before {{other}}, but {{other}} loads earlier
health.incompatible: {{mod}} is marked incompatible with {{other}}, and both are enabled
health.workshop_update_pending: Steam has a newer version of {{mod}}{{published}} that is not downloaded yet. Nothing breaks meanwhile: the game runs the version you have. Steam usually downloads it once the game is closed; if it still waits after that, restart Steam. It matters on a server: servers reject players whose mod versions differ ("Workshop item version is different than the server's").
health.compatible_copy: {{mod}} uses your fixed copy ({{changes}}) instead of the Workshop original, which does not load on your build. Nothing to do. It counts when the game is started from the Studio (from Steam it needs the launch option -modfolders mods,workshop,steam). Once the author updates it, "Back to the original" removes the copy.
health.compatible_copy_unneeded: {{mod}} runs from a compatible copy the Studio made in Zomboid/mods, but the Workshop original now loads on build {{build}} as it is. The copy keeps the older files running and hides the author's updates: go back to the original.
health.shadowed_copy: Another copy of {{mod}} at {{ignored}} is ignored: the game uses the one at {{used}}. Nothing to do.
health.security_executable: {{mod}} ships {{count}} program file(s): {{files}}{{more}}. A program in a mod runs with your rights, outside the game's Lua; keep the mod only if you trust its author. Nothing here says the file is harmful.
health.security_script: {{mod}} ships {{count}} script(s): {{files}}{{more}}. A script in a mod folder runs only if you run it yourself (these are usually the author's build helpers); nothing to do unless you open them.
health.security_java: {{mod}} carries Java code that can {{rules}} ({{where}}{{more}}). Build 42 runs a mod's Java with your rights, through ZombieBuddy, which asks before loading a new jar. Many mods do this for good reasons; keep the mod only if you trust its author.
health.java_patch_overlap_method: {{mods}} each carry Java that changes the method {{methods}} of {{class}}. Whether they clash depends on what each patch does, which the Studio cannot tell from the jar: patches that add code to a method stack, one after the other.{{replace}}{{byCode}} Nothing to do unless this part of the game misbehaves; then try without one of them.
health.java_patch_overlap_methods: {{mods}} each carry Java that changes the methods {{methods}} of {{class}}. Whether they clash depends on what each patch does, which the Studio cannot tell from the jar: patches that add code to a method stack, one after the other.{{replace}}{{byCode}} Nothing to do unless this part of the game misbehaves; then try without one of them.
health.java_patch_overlap_class: {{mods}} each carry Java that changes {{class}}, in different methods ({{detail}}). Neither changes the method the other changes; whether they get along still depends on what each does.{{byCode}} Nothing to do.
health.security_lua: {{mod}}'s Lua does things the game's own scripts never do: {{rules}} ({{where}}{{more}}). The game's Lua cannot run programs or reach the internet by itself, so this is odd rather than dangerous; the file says what it is for.
health.updated_since_last_play: {{n}} active mods were updated since you last played: {{mods}}{{andMore}}. If a save misbehaves, start with these.
health.user_rule_order: You asked for {{mod}} to load after {{after}}{{note}}, and it comes before it in the list
health.community_rule_order_rules: The Studio's rules have it that {{mod}} loads after {{after}}{{note}}{{sourceText}}, and it comes before it in the list
health.community_incompatible_rules: The Studio's rules have it that {{mod}} and {{other}} do not go together{{note}}{{sourceText}}, and both are on
health.community_rule_order_index: The notes the Studio ships with have it that {{mod}} loads after {{after}} ({{note}}{{seen}}), and it comes before it in the list
health.community_incompatible_index: The notes the Studio ships with have it that {{mod}} and {{other}} do not go together ({{note}}{{seen}}), and both are on
health.community_known_issue: {{mod}} has a known issue, per the notes the Studio ships with: {{title}}{{evidence}}{{note}}{{how}} [{{seen}}]
health.learned_issue: Learned on this PC: {{mod}} gave the same error in {{seen}} of {{on}} of your sessions with this version (the last on {{last}}): {{what}}{{evidence}}. If it gets in your way, switch it off until its author updates it; once it no longer happens, the button hides it
health.community_successor: {{mod}} has a version for this build, per the notes the Studio ships with: {{successor}}{{note}}
health.package_built_for_other_list: {{package}} was built with a different list: {{missing}}{{sep}}{{extra}}. A package is a mod of its own, so it shows in every profile; its merges only settle the mods it was built with. The blue button rebuilds it for this list (the same as Update patch in the Mod Merger); switching it off in this profile is the other way.
health.definition: {{losers}} and {{winner}} {{all}} set {{properties}} on {{what}}, in different files ({{files}}). The game applies {{each}} to the same {{things}}, so everything else each of them sets is kept; only {{props}} decided by the load order, and {{winner}} loads last.{{example}}{{settled}}
health.definition_nested: {{losers}} and {{winner}} all declare {{what}}, in different files ({{files}}), and their contents differ. What differs is inside nested blocks, which the Studio does not compare, so it cannot say what is at stake here — only that {{winner}} loads last.{{settled}}
health.script_definition_conflict_more: {{left}} more things, across {{pairs}} other pairs of mods, have a property two mods set differently. Whichever mod loads last decides each one.
health.translation: {{losers}} and {{winner}} name {{what}} differently in {{lang}} ({{category}}).{{example}} The game reads every mod's translations and keeps the last loaded, so {{winner}}'s words show today.{{settled}}
health.file_conflict: {{others}} and {{winner}} both ship {{path}}. Without a merge the game only uses {{winner}}'s copy, so {{others}}'s version is ignored. {{how}}{{checked}}
health.community_unneeded: {{mod}} is no longer needed from build {{since}}, per the notes the Studio ships with: {{who}}{{note}}. {{safe}}
health.function_overridden: {{winner}} replaces the game's {{function}} ({{place}}) after {{cut}} changed it, so that change never runs. {{how}}{{checked}}
health.file_conflict_stale: {{path}} was merged, but {{mods}} changed since. Merge it again so the package matches the current versions.
health.package_file_stale: {{package}} carries a copy of {{path}} made on {{copyDate}}, and {{mod}} changed its own file on {{modDate}}. The game reads the copy, so that change never runs, and the copy may call things the new version no longer has. Take the file out of the package, or patch the new version in the Merger.
health.package_file_differs: {{package}} carries a copy of {{path}} that is not what {{mod}} ships, and {{mod}} is the only mod in this list with that file. Either a merge made when another mod shipped it too (that mod is off now), or a patch of yours. If the merge is no longer needed, take it out: the game then reads {{mod}}'s own file.
health.package_file_orphan: {{package}} carries {{path}} (copied on {{copyDate}}), and no mod in this list ships that file. It loads anyway. If it is a patch of yours it is fine there; if it came from a mod that is off or gone, take it out.
health.server_mod_not_installed: Mods= lists {{entry}}, which is not installed on this machine. If the server does not have it either, it will not load.
health.server_item_missing: {{mod}} is in Mods= but its Workshop id {{item}} is not in WorkshopItems=, so the server never downloads it and the mod is missing in game.
health.server_item_unreachable_copy: WorkshopItems= has {{item}} ({{mods}}), which a server with Steam cannot download (no longer public: removed, made private or hidden, or Steam refused it). The server stops at boot on it. When the Studio starts it with Steam, it leaves the item out of WorkshopItems= and the server runs the copy in Zomboid/mods.
health.server_item_unreachable_will_copy: WorkshopItems= has {{item}} ({{mods}}), which a server with Steam cannot download (no longer public: removed, made private or hidden, or Steam refused it). The server stops at boot on it. When the Studio starts it with Steam, it copies {{mods}} from this PC's Workshop folder into Zomboid/mods and leaves the item out of WorkshopItems=.
health.server_item_unreachable_lost: WorkshopItems= has {{item}}, which a server with Steam cannot download (no longer public: removed, made private or hidden, or Steam refused it), and this PC does not have it either. The server stops at boot on it. When the Studio starts it with Steam, it leaves the item out of WorkshopItems=; its mods will be missing.
health.server_mod_not_from_workshop: {{mod}} did not come from the Workshop, so the server cannot download it: copy its folder into the server's Zomboid/mods itself.
health.server_mod_not_for_build: {{mod}} cannot be loaded by the build installed here ({{entry}}).
health.server_map_missing: {{mod}} adds the map(s) {{maps}}, which Map= does not list. The mod loads, the map does not.
health.server_item_unused_not_installed: WorkshopItems= has {{item}}, which is not installed here, and nothing in Mods= uses it. The server downloads it and loads nothing from it.
health.server_item_unused_holds_one: WorkshopItems= has {{item}}, which holds {{mods}}, but Mods= does not list it. It is downloaded and never loaded.
health.server_item_unused_holds_many: WorkshopItems= has {{item}}, which holds {{mods}}, but Mods= does not list them. It is downloaded and never loaded.
health.server_base_map_last: Map= ends with {{map}}, which is not one of the game's own maps. The base map (for example Muldraugh, KY) belongs last.
health.server_java_not_approved: {{mod}}: its jar {{jar}} is not approved in ZombieBuddy on this PC yet (new or changed since it was approved). The server only loads approved jars (it has no window to ask), so start the game once with this mod on and allow it in ZombieBuddy's window, then start the server.
health.server_java_denied: {{mod}}: ZombieBuddy was told to refuse {{jar}} on this PC, so the server does not load it either. Allow it from ZombieBuddy's window in the game (or remove its line from ~/.zombie_buddy/mod_approvals.json).
health.server_java_without_zombiebuddy: {{mods}} carry Java code (javaJarFile=), but Mods= has no ZombieBuddy: their jars never load on the server, only their Lua.
health.server_java_no_agent: Mods= has ZombieBuddy, but the game's folder ({{folder}}) has no zbNative.dll: the server starts without ZombieBuddy and no Java mod loads (their Lua does). Start the game once with ZombieBuddy on (it puts zbNative.dll and ZombieBuddy.jar there), then start the server.
health.server_java_no_agent_dedicated: Mods= has ZombieBuddy, but the dedicated server's folder ({{folder}}) has no zbNative.dll: the server starts without ZombieBuddy and no Java mod loads (their Lua does). To have them, copy zbNative.dll and ZombieBuddy.jar from the game's folder ({{game}}) into the dedicated server's folder, or start servers from the game's files.
health.server_java_no_agent_dedicated_nowhere: Mods= has ZombieBuddy, but the dedicated server's folder ({{folder}}) has no zbNative.dll: the server starts without ZombieBuddy and no Java mod loads (their Lua does). mod_named_exception_lua.title: {{mod}}: {{lua}}

mod_named_warning_recursive_require.action: Nothing to do unless something of {{mod}} is missing in game; then tell its author (Save report writes the note).

java_mod_error_zb_main.title: ZombieBuddy could not run {{mod}}'s start-up code
java_mod_error_zb_main.explanation: ZombieBuddy started {{mod}}'s Java (its main) and that code failed; ZombieBuddy went on and loaded its patches. On a dedicated server this is expected for a mod that draws the picture (a server draws nothing). In the game it means what {{mod}} sets up when it starts may be missing.
java_mod_error_zb_main.action: Nothing to do on a dedicated server. In the game, if {{mod}} does not work, update it; its Workshop page often says which version of the game it needs.

door_npc.title: The game's own door code met a missing player (B42)
door_npc.explanation: The game's Java for doors (IsoDoor.ToggleDoorActual) asked a player that does not exist whether it is the local one. That happens when something that is not a player opens a door. The failing code is the game's own.
door_npc.action: Nothing to patch from here: the code that fails is Java. If it floods the log, the lines under it say what moved through the door.

door_npc_zombie.title: A zombie opened a door: an error in the game's own door code (B42)
door_npc_zombie.explanation: A zombie opened a door, and the game's Java (IsoDoor.ToggleDoorActual) then asked the player who opened it whether they are the local one, to play the tension music. A zombie is no player, so that question fails. The door is already open when it does: only that music cue and the door's opening animation are skipped. The failing code is the game's own.
door_npc_zombie.action: Nothing to do: the door opens as it should.

item_too_big.title: The game ran out of room packing something into bytes
item_too_big.explanation: The game packs things into a buffer of bytes (an item to save it, or an object turned into an item) and this one held more than the buffer has room for. One known case is a mod asking a body on the ground for its item (IsoDeadBody:getItem), which packs the whole body with everything it carries. The lines under this one in the log say which code asked.
item_too_big.action: If a mod is named next to this line, that mod is where to look. On its own this line does not say whether anything was lost.

bandits_room.title: Bandits Week One: a room program read the room of a tile that has none
bandits_room.explanation: Bandits Week One's BWORoomPrograms.lua asks a tile for its room and then for the room's name without checking that the tile has a room; outdoors it has none, and the script stops there.
bandits_room.action: Its author is the one to fix it (a missing check for no room). If it repeats and bothers you, switching the mod off is the way to tell whether it matters in your game.

save_item_missing.title: An item in the save could not be loaded
save_item_missing.explanation: Loading the save, the game met an item it cannot create any more (the line just above, "cannot create item", names it and its mod). When that item is a part attached to a weapon, the game drops the whole weapon that carried it, not only the part.
save_item_missing.action: If it matters: leave without saving, or restore a backup of the save, and switch the mod named on the line above back on before loading again. Once the game saves, the item is gone.

translator_text.title: A text has a % sign the game cannot format
translator_text.explanation: A translated text has a % that is not written %%, so Java's text formatting cannot read it. The game shows the text as it is and carries on. The text: {{keys}}. {{whose}}
translator_text.action: Nothing to do to play. When a mod ships the text, the fix is in its translation file (% written as %%); Save report names the mod, the file and the line.

windows_low_memory.title: The game closed while Windows was out of memory
windows_low_memory.explanation: At {{when}} Windows reported the whole PC out of memory: {{charge}} of {{limit}} GB committed (RAM {{ram}} GB plus the page file); the game held {{game}} GB{{others}}. The game crashed within moments of that. The limit that ran out is the PC's, not the game's Java heap (-Xmx).
windows_low_memory.action: A bigger page file (Windows > System > About > Advanced system settings > Performance > Virtual memory: system managed, or 16 to 32 GB), closing browsers and other big programs before playing, and fewer memory-hungry Java mods. Diagnostics > Game > Memory keeps the last 14 days.

ui_draw_reload.title: A window ran before the class it is built on existed
ui_draw_reload.explanation: A window ran its {{method}} and the class it is built on was not there at that moment. This is usual for a frame or two while the game loads its Lua again (a save loading, back to the menu). If the same line repeats every frame, the class never exists and the window is broken.
ui_draw_reload.action: A few of these around a reload: nothing to do. Hundreds of them: the mod named next to this line is where to look.

nil_table.title: A script used something that was not there (nil)
nil_table.explanation: A script read or called "{{key}}" on a value that was nil at that moment. The file and the line are in the stack next to this line in the log.
nil_table.action: If a mod is named next to this line, that mod's file is where to look. The line alone does not say what stopped working.

java_mod_error.title: {{mod}} wrote an error of its own to the log

java_mod_error.action: Nothing to do: the mod handled it itself, and the line says how. If what the line names is missing in game, Save report makes a text for its author (the Studio cannot change a mod's Java).

java_npe.title: Java met a missing value (NullPointerException)

java_npe.action: Nothing to apply from here. If it repeats and something misbehaves in game, the lines under it name who called that code.

kahlua.title: A Lua script raised an error itself

kahlua.action: Nothing to do unless something misbehaves in game; then the lines next to this one name the file.

mod_named_warning.action: The game named {{mod}} here and carried on. Nothing to do unless something in that mod misbehaves in game; then this line is where to look.

mod_named_warning_require.title: {{mod}} asked for a file that is not there
mod_named_warning_require.explanation: {{mod}} asked for the file {{file}} (require), and the game found it neither in its own files nor in any mod that is on. Often it is a part meant for another mod you do not have (a compatibility file), and the rest of {{mod}} works.
mod_named_warning_require.action: Nothing to do unless something of {{mod}} is missing in game; then its Workshop page may name a mod it needs without listing it as required.

mod_named_warning_require_moved.title: {{mod}} asked for a game file by its old path
mod_named_warning_require_moved.explanation: {{mod}} asked for {{file}} (require), the path that file had before Build 42 moved it; the game has it now at {{moved_to}}. The game loads its own Lua before any mod's, so the file has already run and the rest of {{mod}} works.
mod_named_warning_require_moved.action: Nothing to do: this line is only noise. Unless an error from {{mod}} follows it in the log; then a compatible copy (Diagnostics) asks for the new path.

connection_lost.title: The connection to the server was gone while joining
connection_lost.explanation: While joining, the game tried to use its connection to the server (to report a missing mod, in the case seen) and the connection was already closed. It is the game's own code, not a mod's.
connection_lost.action: Join again. If a "required mod ... not found" line comes back just before this one, that mod is not installed for this game.

translator_text_missing.title: A text has a placeholder and was given no value
translator_text_missing.explanation: A translated text has a placeholder (%1, %s) and the code that asked for it passed no value. The game shows the text with the placeholder still in it and carries on. The text: {{keys}}. {{whose}}
translator_text_missing.action: Nothing to do to play. Save report names the key and, when a mod ships it, the mod and the file.

mod_named_exception_above.title: {{mod}} was named just above this line
mod_named_exception_above.action: This line names no mod: {{mod}} is in the stack frame the game printed just above it, so the error came up while that mod's code was running. Whether the mod is the cause, the lines around it in the log say.

mod_named_warning_above.title: {{mod}} was named just above this line
mod_named_warning_above.action: This line names no mod: {{mod}} is in the stack frame the game printed just above it, so the error came up while that mod's code was running. Whether the mod is the cause, the lines around it in the log say.

windows_low_memory_nogame.title: The game closed while Windows was out of memory
windows_low_memory_nogame.explanation: At {{when}} Windows reported the whole PC out of memory: {{charge}} of {{limit}} GB committed (RAM {{ram}} GB plus the page file){{others}}. The game crashed within moments of that. The limit that ran out is the PC's, not the game's Java heap (-Xmx).
windows_low_memory_nogame.action: A bigger page file (Windows > System > About > Advanced system settings > Performance > Virtual memory: system managed, or 16 to 32 GB), closing browsers and other big programs before playing, and fewer memory-hungry Java mods. Diagnostics > Game > Memory keeps the last 14 days.

java_out_of_memory.title: The game's Java could not get more memory
java_out_of_memory.explanation: Java asked for memory and got none (OutOfMemoryError). This one is not the Java heap limit: it is memory outside it, which runs out when the PC itself is short. The game usually closes or stops responding after this.
java_out_of_memory.action: Close other big programs before playing. Diagnostics > Game > Memory shows what the PC had; raising the Java limit does not help with this one.

java_out_of_memory_heap.title: The game's Java ran out of the memory it was given
java_out_of_memory_heap.explanation: Java reported "Java heap space": the game used all the memory its Java is allowed (the -Xmx limit). The game usually closes or stops responding after this.
java_out_of_memory_heap.action: Diagnostics > Game > Memory shows the limit, what the PC has, and lets you raise it for the next start.

translator_text_many.title: {{count}} texts have a % sign the game cannot format
translator_text_many.explanation: {{count}} translated texts have a % that is not written %%, so Java's text formatting cannot read them. The game shows each text as it is and carries on. The texts: {{keys}}{{more}}. {{whose}}
translator_text_many.action: Nothing to do to play. When a mod ships the texts, the fix is in its translation files (% written as %%); Save report names the mod, the file and the line of the first one.

translator_text_missing_many.title: {{count}} texts have a placeholder and were given no value
translator_text_missing_many.explanation: {{count}} translated texts have a placeholder (%1, %s) and the code that asked for them passed no value. The game shows each text with the placeholder still in it and carries on. The texts: {{keys}}{{more}}. {{whose}}
translator_text_missing_many.action: Nothing to do to play. Save report names the first key and, when a mod ships it, the mod and the file.

java_patch_failed.title: A Java patch to {{short}} could not be applied
java_patch_failed.explanation: A mod's Java change to {{short}}, part of the game, no longer fits: the method it changes is different now, usually after an update (ZombieBuddy said: "{{why}}"). That change is missing in game; the game itself carries on. Mods with a change to that method: {{suspects}}. Other mods' changes to {{short}} that came after it can be missing too.
java_patch_failed.action: Nothing to do to play. If what the named mod does matters to you, keep it and wait for its author to update it (Save report writes the note for them); if not, switch it off, and the other mods' changes to this class apply. When no mod is named, the Studio could not tell which of those it is.

java_patch_failed_mod.title: A Java patch to {{short}} could not be applied
java_patch_failed_mod.explanation: A mod's Java change to {{short}}, part of another mod's code, no longer fits: the method it changes is different now, usually after an update (ZombieBuddy said: "{{why}}"). That change is missing in game; the game itself carries on. Mods with a change to that method: {{suspects}}. Other mods' changes to {{short}} that came after it can be missing too.
java_patch_failed_mod.action: Nothing to do to play. If what the named mod does matters to you, keep it and wait for its author to update it (Save report writes the note for them); if not, switch it off, and the other mods' changes to this class apply. When no mod is named, the Studio could not tell which of those it is.

java_mod_turned_off.title: {{mod}} switched itself off
java_mod_turned_off.explanation: {{mod}} wrote "{{what}}" (in the log it signs as [{{tag}}]): it stopped its own work for the rest of this session. The game carries on without it.
java_mod_turned_off.action: If it happens every session, it does not work with what is installed now, usually after an update of the game or of the mod it builds on. Switch it off until its author updates it; its Workshop page often already says so.

java_shader_failed.title: A shader of {{mod}} did not compile
java_shader_failed.explanation: {{mod}} could not build a shader; the line says why. What that shader draws is missing.
java_shader_failed.action: A name a shader expects but nobody defines is usually given by an addon of that mod. If another card says an addon switched itself off this session, that addon is the one to switch off or update.

java_shader_failed_undefined.title: A shader of {{mod}} did not compile
java_shader_failed_undefined.explanation: {{mod}} could not build a shader: it uses "{{name}}", which was not defined when it compiled. What that shader draws is missing.
java_shader_failed_undefined.action: A name a shader expects but nobody defines is usually given by an addon of that mod. If another card says an addon switched itself off this session, that addon is the one to switch off or update.

java_shader_failed_addon.title: A shader of {{mod}} did not compile
java_shader_failed_addon.explanation: {{mod}} could not build a shader: it uses "{{name}}", which was not defined when it compiled. Shader code that uses "{{name}}" is in {{addon}}'s jar (an addon that adds to {{mod}}'s shaders), so that is the likely source, perhaps made for another version of {{mod}}. What that shader draws is missing.
java_shader_failed_addon.action: Nothing breaks the game; that part of the picture (often the lighting) is missing or wrong. If it bothers you, switch {{addon}} off or update it, and see whether this card goes away; {{mod}} works without it.

java_addon_incompatible.title: {{mod}} does not fit this version of {{host}}
java_addon_incompatible.explanation: {{host}} says its addon [{{tag}}] does not fit it: "{{what}}". The shaders that addon changes do not build, and {{host}} may switch itself off for it (a card of its own says so).
java_addon_incompatible.action: Switch the addon off until its author updates it for this version of {{host}}; {{host}} works without it.

saves.title: Saves
saves.blurb: PZ Mod Studio backs a save up when you leave it, before it loads with mods that changed since its last session, and before its mod list is changed. Each backup is a zip read back after it is written. The newest {{keep}} automatic backups of each save are kept; the ones you make or pin stay until you remove them.

frames.title: Frames and hitches
frames.blurb: Frame times, hitches, chunks loaded and, per mod, the Lua handlers that cost the most, with the file and the line. The Studio's profiler counts them while you play (Measure, above); measurements another mod leaves in the console are read too.
frames.needsMod: Nothing to show yet. Press Measure above and play a few minutes: the profiler counts every frame and what the game loaded.
frames.needsPlay: The profiler is on, but no frame has been counted yet: open the game and play a few minutes.
frames.ownNote: Counted by the Studio's profiler. The table lists the mods one of whose handlers held a single frame 25 ms or more; the garbage collector and the engine's own time are not Lua and are not attributed.
frames.nothingYet: No minute measured yet. Play a minute and read again.
frames.minutesTitle: One line a minute of play; the menu does not count

frames.note: A mod that is not among the ten costliest of a minute is not in that minute's line, so a mod that appears in few minutes is cheap most of the time. The engine's own chunk loading is not Lua and does not appear per mod. Source: measurements found in the console.

gameTime.title: Game time per mod
gameTime.blurb: Which mods slow the game down while you play: every event handler of every mod (OnTick, OnPlayerUpdate, OnZombieUpdate...) timed by the game itself and added up per mod. "Measure" puts a small Studio mod first in your list and in the save you played last; start the game, play a few minutes as usual, and the numbers appear here.
gameTime.onWithSave: Measuring is on: the profiler is first in your mod list and in the save {{save}}. It starts with the next game launch; restart the game if it is running.
gameTime.onNoSave: Measuring is on: the profiler is first in your mod list (no save found to add it to). It starts with the next game launch.
gameTime.total: all mods: {{pct}} % of the game's time
gameTime.viaPackage: Part of this time is the mod's code merged into a Studio package.
gameTime.waiting: No numbers yet: start the game (restart it if it was running) and they arrive every 5 seconds.
gameTime.how: The % is the share of real time the mod's Lua took (60 FPS leaves 16.7 ms a frame): its event handlers, and the render / prerender / update of its windows, bars and timed actions (named Class:render). Each counts its own time only: a mod's render that calls the game's counts without the game's part. A long single call is a hitch you see as a freeze. The game's clock counts whole milliseconds, so a short handler is measured on average over many calls; give it a minute or two. Stop measuring when you are done: the profiler adds a little time of its own to every handler.

bootTime.title: Game start
bootTime.blurb: How long the game took to reach the main menu, stage by stage, from the log every launch leaves. Set beside your usual start with about as many mods, so a mod that adds seconds shows.
bootTime.none: No start to show yet: the game writes it the first time it reaches the main menu.
bootTime.slowerNote: A stage in amber took much longer than usual. The same mods with a slow stage once is usually the PC doing something else at the time (a disk busy, a build, an update); every start slow there since some day points at what changed that day.

gameMemory.title: Game memory
gameMemory.blurb: Project Zomboid runs on Java, which never uses more memory than its launch file allows (-Xmx in ProjectZomboid64.json). With many mods the game's own value runs short: the game stutters while Java frees memory over and over, and in the end closes with an out-of-memory error.

gameMemory.windowsLog_one: Windows closed the game for lack of memory {{count}} time in the last 14 days:
gameMemory.windowsLog_other: Windows closed the game for lack of memory {{count}} times in the last 14 days:
gameMemory.windowsLogGame: game {{game}} GB, {{charge}} of {{limit}} GB in all
gameMemory.windowsAdvice: This is not the game's Java heap (-Xmx above): the game's native side and Java mods grow past it. What helps: a bigger page file (Windows > System > About > Advanced system settings > Performance > Virtual memory: system managed, or 16 to 32 GB), closing browsers and other big programs before playing, and fewer memory-hungry Java mods.
gameMemory.ranOut_one: The game ran out of memory in {{count}} of the last sessions ({{logs}}): give it more.
gameMemory.ranOut_other: The game ran out of memory in {{count}} of the last sessions ({{logs}}): give it more.

gameMemory.closeGame: Close the game to change it: it keeps its launch file open.
gameMemory.done: Done: the profile {{name}} gives the game {{gb}} GB from its next start. A copy of the launch file before the change is in PZModStudio_Backups.
gameMemory.how: Takes effect the next time the game starts. More is not always better: past what the mods need, Java takes longer each time it cleans up, and Windows, the graphics driver and the game's own native side need the rest of the memory, so the Studio offers up to half of the PC's ({{max}} GB). A game update can put its own value back; the Studio restores yours when it starts the game.

gameMemory.profileNone: The profile {{name}} has no value of its own yet: it takes the last one chosen. Apply one and it keeps it; each profile can have its own.

welcome.title: Welcome to PZ Mod Studio
welcome.body: A mod manager for Project Zomboid that also fixes what breaks. This tour walks through every screen with the real screen behind it; go on with Next or the arrow keys, and close it whenever you like.
points: What the Studio changes (the game's mod list, your saves, launch files) it backs up first.
It never deletes anything without asking, and what it removes goes to the Recycle Bin or can be undone.
It does not change your mods' files: fixes go into a package of its own that loads last.

folders.title: Your folders
folders.body: First things first: where the game is and where your mods are. The Studio finds them itself. If one says "Not found", pick it with the Browse... button on the Settings screen behind this card.
points: The game folder is where ProjectZomboid64.exe is.
The Workshop folder is where Steam downloads the mods you subscribe to.
The Zomboid folder (in your user folder) holds saves, local mods and the game's logs.

profiles.title: Profiles
profiles.body: A profile is a named mod list: which mods belong to it, which are on, and their load order. Switch between them with one click and the game starts with those mods.
points: One profile per play style or per server: each with its own mods and saves.
Turning a profile on writes its mods into the list the game reads (default.txt).
Share a profile as a .pzpack file; whoever opens it subscribes to what they lack.

modList.title: Mod List
modList.body: Your installed mods: switch them on and off and order them. Every change is saved at once to the active profile and the game's list.
points: Every problem Diagnostics finds shows as a chip on the row, with the fix beside it.
"Auto-Sort Dependencies" puts each mod after what it needs, the way the game does.
Filters, groups, notes, right-click and undo for big lists.

health.title: Diagnostics
health.body: What the app knows about your mods, the game and the server, in three parts, with a step-by-step guide on the front page for when you do not know where to start.
points: Mods: checks your list with the game's own rules. Problems: missing or switched-off requirements, wrong order, mods your build can't load, incompatible pairs. Many are fixed with one button.
Conflicts: two mods shipping the same file or item; merge them or pick one.

Game: what it uses now (memory, CPU, which screen it is on), its memory limit, how long it takes to start, frames and disk. Server: the server running on this PC and, during a multiplayer test, its players.

monitor.title: Monitor Center
monitor.body: Start the game from here and read its log as it runs. Every error becomes a card naming the mod behind it and what you can do.
points: Red cards for exceptions, amber for warnings the game carried on through.
Many cards carry the fix (an old require path, patching a file) or a report to hand to the author.
"Find the mod that does it" halves the list, tests and repeats until it finds the culprit.

saves.title: Saves
saves.body: Your saves, by profile, and their backups. The Studio backs a save up when you leave it, before it loads with changed mods, and before another one is restored.
points: Restore puts a save back to a backup, keeping the current one first so it can be undone.
A line says when a save's mods changed since its last session, or when one is not installed.
Servers' saves show with their address and the profile you joined with.

whatsNew.title: What's New
whatsNew.body: Workshop mods updated since you last played, with their change notes. Read it before loading a running save.
points: It shows each update's change notes, to read before you load a save.
You can keep a mod's version before it updates and go back to it.

browse.title: Browse Mods
browse.body: Search the Steam Workshop and Nexus Mods without leaving the Studio, subscribe, and make your own lists.
points: Subscribing also offers what the mod needs.
Workshop collections: see which ones you lack and make a profile from them.
Install a .zip or folder you downloaded elsewhere (Nexus, GitHub, Discord).

maps.title: Maps
maps.body: The game's world with all your map mods on top: which part of Knox Country each one changes and where two fight over the same ground.

merger.title: Mod Merger
merger.body: When two mods change the same file, the game uses only one. Combine them here, or patch a bug in a mod's file, without touching the mod.
points: Your choices go into a package of your own that loads last, so the game reads your version.
Safe cases merge by themselves from Diagnostics; you come here for the rest.

servers.title: Servers
servers.body: Three tabs: Public servers, My servers and Host a server of your own.
points: Join: find servers, see which mods they load and join; make a profile from a server's mods.
Host: run a dedicated server from this PC with your mods in sync, players, quick settings and Discord.

link.title: The Studio Link mod, inside the game
link.body: A small mod the Studio installs and keeps on in every profile. It is the app's part inside the game.
points: The game's MODS button opens its own Mods screen, with the active profile, search and filters.
It warns before loading a save whose mods changed, and asks for the backup.
On a server the game loads only the server's mods, so the Link does not run there.

settings.title: Settings
settings.body: Folders, language, notices, how the Studio starts, app updates, and the Build 42 fixes.
points: Options are saved as soon as you change them.
Developer features are switched on here.

developer.title: For mod makers
developer.body: With "Developer features" on in Settings, the Developer screen shows, and the MCP tab for connecting AI agents.
points: Make a new mod, check every Lua and script file of it before the game does.
Start the game with only that mod and reload its Lua while the game runs.
Multiplayer check: calls that on a server have to go through the server.

help.title: If you get stuck
help.body: Click "?" at the bottom right (or F1) on any screen for its help page. This tour opens from there too.
points: Monitor cards and Diagnostics rows have "Copy for an assistant": paste it into any AI chat and it has everything needed.
Start with Diagnostics: if it is clean, your list loads.

simpleProfiles.title: Make or choose a profile
simpleProfiles.body: A profile is your list of mods: which are on and in what order. Make one (it can start with the mods you have on now) or switch one on. The game starts with its mods.
points: You can have several: one per play style or per server.
Your saves are kept: switching profiles does not delete anything.

play.title: Play
play.body: Home has the Play button and, once you have played, Continue for your last game. The check-up tells you in one line whether there is something to fix first.
points: Green: nothing to do, just play.
Red: press "See what to do"; each problem has one button that fixes it.
You are in Simple mode. For every tool, switch to Complete at the foot of the left bar or in Settings.

launch.title: Custom launch
launch.blurb: Where the game goes as soon as it starts. The launch button remembers it until you pick another place.
launch.noServers: No kept servers. Add them in Servers (My servers).
launch.saveHow: The game opens and, at the main menu, the Studio Link mod loads this save, with the same notices and backup as Continue. Then comes the game's black "click to start" screen.
launch.serverHow: Like Join in Servers: with the server's kept password and your username. The game loads the server's mods.

guide.title: What this screen is
guide.touches: What it changes on your PC

health.what: Checks your mod list the way the game will read it and tells you what to do about each thing: act, worth doing, good to know, or already fixed by the Studio.
health.who: Yes, anyone. Look at it before playing if you changed mods or the game updated.
health.touches: Looking changes nothing. Each button says below it what it changes before you press it, and almost everything can be undone.
health.flow: The coloured tags in the Mod List are these same findings: a click on one brings you straight to it.

merger.what: When two mods ship the same file, the game uses only one and the other's changes are lost. Here a package is made that combines both.
merger.who: Only if Diagnostics sends you here (Conflicts tab) or you want to fix a file by hand. If you just play and Diagnostics shows no conflicts, you don't need it.
merger.touches: Makes a Studio mod (Z_PZModStudio_…) in Zomboid/mods that loads last and wins. The original mods are not touched: switching the package off or deleting it undoes it.
merger.flow: Mod List → conflict tag → Diagnostics, Conflicts tab → "Merge automatically" (done for you) or "Open in the Merger" (you choose, here).

developer.what: Tools for people who make mods: check a mod's files, see whether it uses things your game build does not have, test it alone, translate it and upload it to the Workshop.
developer.who: If you just play, no. It is for making or fixing a mod.
developer.touches: Checking files, the build check and Multiplayer only read. "Start the game with only this mod" changes your list while the game is open and puts it back when it closes. "New mod" makes a folder in Zomboid/mods.

doctorChat.title: Ask the Doctor
doctorChat.blurb: It answers with what this PC learned and the app's tools, with no AI: each answer says where it comes from. Anything that changes something asks you first.

mode.label: View
mode.simpleHint: Only what you need to play with mods. Everything else is one click away.
mode.advancedHint: Every screen and tool of the Studio.

settings.title: How much of the Studio to show
settings.blurb: Simple shows what you need to play with mods. Complete shows every screen. Nothing is deleted or switched off when you change: you can go back and forth whenever you like.
settings.simple: Home with Play, your mods (on/off, order, Auto-Sort), profiles, Explore, saves, and in Diagnostics only what you need to fix, with one button each.
settings.advanced: Everything: Monitor, What's new, Maps, Merger, Servers, Developer, every Diagnostics tab and the AI tools.
settings.headerBlurb: Where your game and mods live, which warnings you see, and the app.

home.continueTitle: Opens the game and loads {{world}}, your last game with this profile.
home.actHint: You need to act: a mod will not load or something breaks until you fix it.
home.ok: Your mods are in order: nothing to do
home.optional_one: You can play. 1 optional suggestion (the game works without it) is in Complete mode.
home.optional_other: You can play. {{count}} optional suggestions (the game works without them) are in Complete mode.
home.modsHint: Switch mods on and off and put them in order (or let the Studio order them).
home.browseHint: Find and subscribe to Workshop mods.
home.moreInComplete: This is Simple mode. Merger, Monitor, Servers, Maps and the other tools are in Complete mode.
home.noModsOn: No mods are on in this profile yet: the game would start without mods.
home.gameOpenLine: The game is open. The first time with new mods it takes a few minutes to load. You can leave the Studio open in the background.

health.nothingToAct: Nothing to fix: your mods are ready to play.
health.optionalHidden_one: 1 optional suggestion is hidden (the game works without it).
health.optionalHidden_other: {{count}} optional suggestions are hidden (the game works without them).
health.nothingToDoHidden_one: 1 more is only good to know or already fixed by the Studio: nothing to do.
health.nothingToDoHidden_other: {{count}} more are only good to know or already fixed by the Studio: nothing to do.
health.intro: Only what you need to fix for your mods to load properly, each with its button. The optional ones and the ones that ask for nothing are counted below.
health.fixAllTitle: Makes the safe fixes of the list above (switching on what is missing and ordering). The hidden optional suggestions are left alone.
health.mergerExplain: Two mods change the same thing and the game uses only one: the one of the mod that loads last. Choosing what stays from each is done in the Complete view.
health.pickOne: Pick which of the two to switch off: the other stays on.
health.checksAgain: The Studio checks again by itself: anything left to do shows below.
health.copyReady: The fixed copy of {{name}} is ready.
health.copyNext: Play with the Studio's Play button so the game uses the copy (the Workshop original stays as it was). Try it in a new game first.
health.copyMayBreak_one: Note: 1 thing could not be fixed in the copy; if the mod fails in the game, switch it off.
health.copyMayBreak_other: Note: {{count}} things could not be fixed in the copy; if the mod fails in the game, switch it off.
health.homeOptional_one: Nothing to fix. There is 1 optional suggestion (the game runs without it) in Complete.
health.homeOptional_other: Nothing to fix. There are {{count}} optional suggestions (the game runs without them) in Complete.

offer.title: There is a Simple view with just what you need to play: give it a try.
offer.body: It shows Home with Play, your mods and only the problems you need to fix. Nothing is deleted or switched off, and Complete is one click away at the foot of the left bar.
offer.noTitle: You stay in Complete and this note does not come back. Simple stays at the foot of the left bar and in Settings.

modList.title: Mod List
modList.blurb: Switch on the ones you want to use. Order matters: the one at the top loads first. If you do not know the right order, press "Auto-Sort".
modList.missing: A mod needs one you do not have
modList.missingTitle: You need to act: a mod needs another one you do not have. Click to go to each; its red mark has the button to find it on the Workshop.
modList.depsOff: Need a mod that is off
modList.depsOffTitle: You need to act: a mod needs another one that is switched off. Click to go to each; its red mark has the button to switch it on.
modList.incompatibleTitle: You need to act: two mods that are on clash with each other. Click to go to each and switch one of them off.
modList.orderTitle: You need to act: a mod loads before one it needs. Click to go to each, or press "Auto-Sort" to fix them all.
modList.autoSortTitle: Puts each mod after the ones it needs. Everything else stays as you left it, and it can be undone.
modList.loadsLast: BOTTOM: loads last (when two mods change the same thing, this one wins)
modList.sortRule: Each mod now comes after the mods it needs, as the game asks. Everything else kept its order. If you do not like it, press Undo.

sortReason.load_after: {{mod}} goes after {{other}}: its author asks for it.
sortReason.load_before: {{mod}} goes before {{other}}: its author asks for it.
sortReason.rule: {{mod}} goes after {{other}}: you asked for it.
sortReason.index: {{mod}} goes after {{other}}: the Studio knows they work that way.
sortReason.package: {{mod}} goes last: it is a Studio fix and loads after the mods it fixes.

modList.orphans: {{count}} mods you have installed (subscribed on Steam's website, for example) are in no profile. "Add to the profile" adds them to "{{name}}", switched off; "Show them" lets you look first.

profiles.launchFile: Some mods (the ones with Java code, which use ZombieBuddy) are not loaded from the list but from the game's start-up. The Studio sets that start-up to follow this profile, keeping a copy first. Nothing else to do.
profiles.launchFileLater: Some mods (the ones with Java code, which use ZombieBuddy) are loaded from the game's start-up. The game is open, so the Studio sets that start-up as soon as you close it. Nothing else to do.
profiles.launchOut: No longer loads when the game starts
profiles.launchBack: Loads again when the game starts
profiles.outNote: is not on in this profile
profiles.everythingHint: Want every mod you have installed on ({{count}} mods)? It is rarely a good idea: that many mods take long to load and some do not go together.
profiles.everythingChosen: This profile will switch on all {{count}} mods you have installed, at once.

header.NORMAL_FULLSCREEN: Fills the whole screen, as when you open it from Steam.
header.NORMAL_WINDOWED: In a window: you see the game and the Studio at once.

issueText.outside_version_range: {{mod}} is not made for your version of the game ({{build}}): as it is, the game does not load it.
issueText.not_for_build: {{mod}} is not made for your version of the game ({{build}}): as it is, the game does not load it.
issueText.dependency_not_enabled: {{mod}} needs {{dep}}, which you have installed but switched off.
issueText.missing_dependency_plain: {{mod}} needs {{dep}}, which you do not have installed.
issueText.dependency_after: {{mod}} needs {{dep}}, but {{dep}} is further down the list: it has to load first.
issueText.incompatible: {{mod}} and {{other}} do not go together: they cannot both be on.
issueText.require_spaced_copy: {{mod}} has a typo in its files (a space in the list of mods it needs), so the game skips it even though it shows as on. "Make compatible copy" fixes it in a copy; the original stays as it is.
issueText.require_spaced_local: {{mod}} has a typo in its mod.info (a space in the list of mods it needs), so the game skips it even though it shows as on. Take the spaces out of its require= line.
